description: The one definition of 'how much of this machine may a single training run
have'. Before this file the question was answered independently by the bash
installer, its PowerShell twin, the Go CLI, and a fourth 0.75-fraction
policy in node_sizing.py itself — four implementations, none derived from
the others, two of which disagreed by construction.
The installer speaks bash, its twin speaks PowerShell and the CLI speaks
Go, so no consumer can call the Python. Each therefore vendors this file
and replays the golden vectors below through its own reader, in its own
test suite, drift-gated against this repo at a pinned ref. Mutate the
arithmetic without regenerating the vectors and this repo reddens at once;
regenerate them and every consumer's gate reddens. That is the ticket's

overhead.derived_from: tracebloc/client: scripts/tests/control-plane-footprint.sh --print-footprint (the steady-state control plane the chart renders, summed the scheduler's way), client chart 1.9.119
overhead.checked_by: tracebloc/client .github/workflows/envelope-contract-drift.yml compares this pair against a fresh render of the chart; a chart change that moves the render reddens there and is adopted by regenerating this contract
why: What the platform's OWN PODS request on the node a run shares with them:
jobs-manager, the requests proxy, MySQL, the egress proxy, the telemetry
collector -- every Deployment/StatefulSet/DaemonSet the chart installs,
summed from the render (backend#2870). Before contract v3 this was a
typed 1 CPU / 3 GiB that stood in for two different things at once: the
platform pods AND the kubelet, containerd and the Docker VM's daemons,
which k3s never reserved (allocatable == capacity). backend#2460 moved
the second half where it belongs -- kubeReserved / systemReserved /
evictionHard in the installer's kubelet drop-in, measured per platform --
so allocatable itself is now net of it, and subtracting it here again
would count it twice. What is left to subtract is the pods, and that is
a number the chart declares, not one anybody types.
NOT included: the k3s addon pods (coredns, metrics-server, ~140 MiB /
200 m). The installer measures those live on the cluster it is sizing
(_measured_system_requests) and jobs-manager's admission reads the live
steady state; a static number here would be counted twice on the paths
that measure and be stale on the k3s version that moves it.
Because it is derived from the render, a control-plane trim MOVES it:
regenerate this contract, then re-vendor in client and cli. That is how
v3 -> v4 happened: the four-leg load run on backend#2461 sized the
control plane, client#1055 adopted it in chart 1.9.119, and the render
went from 900m / 3136 MiB to 650m / 1792 MiB.
Below this a training run is not worth scheduling, so a machine that
cannot clear it after overhead is reported NON-VIABLE. It is not a clamp:
clamping up is how a machine under per_node_minimum (the 4 GiB WSL2 box,
under the v2/v3 overhead) ended up asked to host an 8 GiB pod that stays
Pending forever.
Memory inside the Docker VM that is NOT a k3d node container and must
survive whatever the nodes are capped to: the k3d serverlb and tools
containers, dockerd/containerd itself, and enough page cache for image
layers. Measured on a live 2-node cluster: serverlb 39.27 MiB + tools
14.69 MiB, plus the daemon and guest kernel outside any container. 1 GiB
is deliberately more than the containers alone -- capping the nodes to
the last byte of the VM starves the runtime that runs them, which is the
same class of failure as not capping them at all.
This is a reserve against the VM, NOT the per-pod platform overhead in
`overhead` above. They stack: overhead is subtracted inside a node,
vm_reserve outside all of them.

topology.question: How many k3d node containers may this VM honestly host, and what is each one's memory cap?
rule: cap    = usable // nodes        (floored -- a cap that rounds up is not a cap)
topology.vm_source: docker info {{.NCPU}} and {{.MemTotal}} -- the container runtime's VM, NOT the host and NOT the sum of node allocatable

why: A node container hosts the platform overhead AND must still clear the
training floor, or nothing schedules on it. Derived, never a fourth
constant. Measured (contract v2, 1 CPU / 3 GiB overhead): capping a node
at 3g -- under the overhead alone -- made both nodes of a live cluster
report |unschedulable. The `exact-floor` vector sits exactly on this
sum and is generated from it, so it moves when the overhead does.

cpu_why: MEASURED on k3d v5.9.0 / k3s v1.35.5 / Docker 29.5.2: capacity.cpu cannot
be capped by ANY container-level mechanism.
* k3d 5.9.0 has no CPU flag at all -- only --servers-memory/--agents-memory.
* docker --cpus=2 sets a CFS quota (cpu.max 200000 100000 in the
* docker --cpuset-cpus=0-4 makes nproc report 5 and capacity.cpu stays 10.
of which any cgroup namespaces. Confirmed against a forced node
de-register/re-register, so it is not a stale node object.
Consequence: memory is made honest by CAPPING, cpu only by having FEWER
NODE CONTAINERS. That is why honest_topology reports cpu_honest rather
than implying the cap closed it, and why collapsing to one node -- the
remedy the GPU path already chose for --gpus=all -- is the general fix.

measured.each_node_uncapped: 10 cpu / 8126672Ki -- byte-identical to the VM MemTotal
measured.capped_3g_each: capacity.memory 3221225Ki per node; sum 6.14 GiB <= 7.75 GiB VM (0.792x)
measured.also_double_counted: ephemeral-storage: 474095688Ki capacity on both nodes, the same VM disk twice

why: The historical fixed envelope, still hardcoded in six physical places
across three repos (_TRAINING_DEFAULT, the ps1's two inline copies, the
chart template's two, DEFAULT_JOB_RESOURCES). Recorded here so those
become readers too. NOTE it is LARGER than the floor: handing it to a
non-viable machine is the sub-8GiB bug, not a safe default.

largest.question: What is the largest run this machine could host?
largest.rule: the single schedulable node maximising (cpu_millicores, memory_bytes) lexicographically
used_by: client installer — sizing the value it writes
cli resources set — clamping the wizard prompt and the fit check
why: A pod's resources all come from ONE node, so this question is
single-node by nature and must never sum across the cluster.
The tie-break is itself a consolidation: bash ranked nodes (memory,
cpu) and cli's nodeLarger ranked them (cpu, memory), so on a cluster of
8c/16Gi + 4c/32Gi the two anchored on different nodes. Nobody chose
that; it fell out of two independent implementations.

every.question: What envelope fits on EVERY schedulable node?
every.rule: minimum cpu_millicores and minimum memory_bytes, taken independently
used_by: client-runtime derive path (DERIVE_JOB_ENVELOPE, off by default)
why: An envelope sized to the biggest node cannot schedule on the smallest.
Independent minima are deliberately conservative — a heterogeneous
cluster with a small system nodepool degrades toward the floor rather
than risking an unschedulable pod.

rendering.Gi: cpu=<whole cores>,memory=<whole GiB>Gi — installer + CLI surface
rendering.Mi: cpu=<whole cores>,memory=<whole MiB>Mi — jobs-manager pod spec
rendering.rounding: always floor; a ceiling that rounds up is not a ceiling
